strengths: The core idea is well executed: constructing explicit part-level correspondence labels from frozen foundation-model patch features (objectness PCA + fine-grained PCA + k-means) and using them as a plug-and-play supervisory signal for existing GCD methods is simple, principled, and clearly differentiated from prior part-aware GCD work (SPTNet's implicit prompts, APL's part queries, PartGCD's GMM decomposition).

Evaluation is unusually thorough: results across four host methods (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx), three backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), six main datasets plus Oxford-Pet and Herbarium19, and comparison against 20 recent methods including ICML'25/CVPR'25/NeurIPS'25 work.

The supplementary ablations are convincing and address the key confounds: foreground-only masking shows the gains are not merely from background suppression (Tab. I); comparison against SD-DINOv2 labels validates the label construction choice (Tab. H); label quality is validated against CUB ground-truth parts (Tab. F); complementarity with implicit part learning is demonstrated (Tab. E); K-estimation robustness is studied (Tab. J/K); computational overhead is quantified (Tab. B) and inference cost is unchanged.

The success/failure per-class analysis (Sec. S4) is a genuinely informative diagnostic: gains concentrate on part-dependent fine-grained species while failures are global-shape-biased classes, with a quantified asymmetry (max drop ~35 pts vs. gains up to 100 pts).

Limitations are honestly and specifically discussed (Sec. S5), including the patch-grid resolution constraint, dependence on ViT patch-token backbones, and the deliberately lightweight PCA-based decomposition; implementation details, hyperparameters, and training budgets are reported, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: There is a circularity concern that is not fully resolved: the part correspondence labels are derived from the same family of frozen DINO patch features that the finetuned backbone starts from, so PartCo is in part distilling the frozen model's part structure into the finetuned model. The foreground-only and SD-DINOv2 ablations mitigate this, but a stronger control (e.g., supervising with labels from a different architecture, or random/degenerate correspondences of equal cluster count) would more directly isolate the value of the part prior itself.

Several design choices are heuristics rather than principled: the choice between 1st- and 2nd-order labels is decided manually by dataset type ('fine-grained vs. generic'), the order-selection criterion is a hand-crafted product of min-centroid-distance and cluster balance, and the mask threshold tau_obj=0.6 is fixed. An automatic selection mechanism would strengthen the claim of a 'versatile framework'.

On generic benchmarks the improvements are modest (CIFAR-10 essentially saturated; some cells regress, e.g., PartCo-SimGCD 'New' on CIFAR100 with DINOv2 drops to 83.0 vs. 87.2 baseline), so the contribution's value is primarily concentrated on fine-grained SSB benchmarks. The claim of 'setting new benchmarks for GCD' is somewhat overstated: PartCo-SelEx (85.5 avg on SSB) is actually slightly below Hyp-SelEx (86.0) on the strongest baseline, which the text acknowledges but the abstract and conclusion do not.

Novelty is moderate: unsupervised part discovery via DINOv2 PCA foreground/background decomposition (cf. MaskCut/LOST-style pipelines) and part-level GCD are both established; the contribution is primarily a well-validated combination, and the contrastive part loss is a fairly standard construction.

The unsupervised part contrastive loss relies on pseudo-labels whose quality interacts with training dynamics (error propagation through part and category pseudo-labels jointly), but no analysis of sensitivity to pseudo-label noise or behavior over training is provided.

strengths: The core idea is simple and practical: distilling part-level correspondence labels (from frozen DINOv2 patch features via PCA + k-means) into existing GCD methods through a part-level contrastive loss. The plug-and-play design adds no inference cost and requires only modest training overhead (Tab. B), which is attractive.

Consistent empirical gains across four host baselines (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx) and three backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), with large improvements on fine-grained benchmarks (e.g., +9.8% average 'All' ACC for PartCo-SimGCD on SSB with DINOv2).

The evaluation goes beyond headline numbers: ablations on label order granularity (Fig. 7, Tab. G), part-label quality against CUB ground-truth parts (Tab. F), background-suppression vs. explicit part correspondence (Tab. I), SD-DINOv2 vs. DINOv2 label construction (Tab. H), K-estimation robustness (Tab. J/K), and an honest success/failure per-class analysis (Tab. L) with a genuine limitations section (S5).

The supplementary distinguishes PartCo from closely related part-based GCD methods (APL, PartGCD, SPTNet) and empirically shows complementarity with SPTNet (Tab. E), supporting the claim that explicit part priors add value beyond implicit part learning.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The framework is essentially PCA + k-means clustering of frozen patch features followed by a standard supervised contrastive loss. Given that APL (CVPR'25) and PartGCD (TMM) already inject part-level information into GCD, the conceptual contribution is incremental; the main novelty is the specific label-construction recipe and the training-only supervision signal.

A significant methodological soft spot: the choice between 1st- and 2nd-order labels is made per-dataset ('datasets with subtle, intra-class differences indicate fine-grained samples' — Sec. 3.1/Fig. 4). This is a dataset-level hyperparameter that requires knowledge of dataset character and cannot be selected from the data alone, weakening the 'seamless, automatic plug-and-play' claim. The k* selection criterion and fixed threshold τ_obj = 0.6 are similarly heuristic and unvalidated in sensitivity.

The strongest SOTA claims are overstated. On the SSB average with DINOv2, PartCo-SelEx (85.5) does not surpass Hyp-SelEx (86.0), and PartCo-SelEx actually loses 'Old' accuracy on CUB (85.1 → 84.5; -0.4% in Fig. 6). On generic datasets, gains are marginal (+0.3-2.2%) and CIFAR10 is essentially saturated. The phrase 'setting new benchmarks for GCD' in the abstract is not supported.

No variance reporting: all results appear to be single runs with no standard deviations or significance tests, despite the accuracy differences between PartCo-SelEx and Hyp-SelEx being within ~0.5 points. This makes the competitiveness claims difficult to assess.

The 'correspondence' framing is somewhat misleading: the labels are cluster IDs from k-means on PCA projections, not verified correspondences across images. The paper's own Tab. F shows ~80%/77.5% agreement with CUB part annotations, with some parts at ~43-50% (forehead), indicating the supervisory signal is noisy; no mechanism handles correspondence ambiguity or occlusion explicitly despite these motivating the work (Fig. 2, Sec. 1).
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a recipe with many heuristic choices (number of PCA components, thresholds, k sweep, loss weighting, projection dimension).

Writing is repetitive, particularly the motivation in Secs. 1 and 3, and several implementation details (e.g., how pseudo-label-based N_c^i is formed early in training when pseudo-labels are unreliable) are under-specified.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated plug-and-play framework: part-level correspondence labels constructed from frozen DINO patch features via PCA + k-means, then distilled into any GCD method through an additional contrastive loss (Eqs. 6-8) with no architectural or inference-time changes. The design is clearly described and easy to reimplement.

Comprehensive empirical validation: consistent gains across four diverse host methods (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx), two backbones (DINOv2/v3) plus a CLIP-only experiment (Tab. D), and six benchmark datasets including long-tailed Herbarium19 (Tab. C). Large absolute improvements on fine-grained data (e.g., +9.8% for PartCo-SimGCD on SSB) with smaller but steady gains on generic data.

Thorough and honest ablations: label quality is validated against CUB's annotated parts (Tab. F, 80.8% agreement); a foreground-only masking ablation (Tab. I) convincingly shows the gains come from explicit part correspondence rather than background suppression; order-level analysis (Fig. 7, Tab. G) and a comparison against SD-DINOv2 label construction (Tab. H) support design choices.

Good supplementary coverage of practical concerns: computational overhead is modest and quantified (Tab. B), inference cost is unchanged, robustness to erroneous K-estimates is studied (Tabs. J-K), and per-class success/failure analysis (Tab. L) with an honest limitations section (S5) discussing patch-grid resolution and CNN incompatibility.
weaknesses: Dataset-dependent manual design choices weaken the 'automatic prior' narrative: the choice between 1st- and 2nd-order labels is made by the authors per dataset (fine-grained vs. generic), and the objectness threshold τ_obj=0.6 is fixed without a sensitivity analysis. A principled or automatic selection criterion for the label order would strengthen the contribution.

Novelty is moderate: DINO patch features are known to cluster into semantic parts, and the supervised contrastive loss (Eq. 6) is standard. The contribution is primarily a careful integration plus extensive benchmarking rather than a new technique; the paper is upfront that PartCo is a training-only supervisory signal, but the methodological depth is limited.

Not uniformly state-of-the-art: on the SSB average with DINOv2, Hyp-SelEx (86.0 'All') slightly exceeds PartCo-SelEx (85.5), and PartCo occasionally hurts 'Old' accuracy (e.g., SelEx 85.1→84.5; CIFAR100 'New' for PartCo-SimGCD drops to 83.0). The paper's claim is correctly softened to 'outperforming most existing methods', but per-split regressions deserve more discussion.

Evaluation rigor gaps: results appear to be single runs without variance or significance testing, and the k* selection heuristic (maximizing min centroid distance × cluster balance) is only partially ablated. Generalization is only tested on standard GCD benchmarks; no experiments under domain shift or with very heterogeneous datasets.

Presentation issues: Sec. 2/3 background re-explains well-known baselines at length, while some essential details (e.g., full k* candidate set, behavior when background masking fails) are deferred to supplementary material; Table 1's negative results for PartCo-SelEx 'Old' are not highlighted in the main text.
